entries.onMind: the hang test at first light
entries.text: Dreamed I hung off the splint and it didn't tick, and when I looked down the bench was a long way under me. Woke with both hands closed tight on the bedroll like it was cord.
entries.title: The splint held

entries.text: Sat up and the smoke past the water was already going, thin and steady over the trees. Whoever it is was up before me again.
entries.title: Already smoking

entries.reason: He eats before testing anything; shaky hands make bad readings.
entries.text: Ate a heel of the loaf and a thumb of cheese on the crate. Left in the cloth: half a loaf, the cheese wedge, one strip of jerky, nine apple rings.
entries.title: Counting the bundle

entries.text: Hung off the splinted side spar with my whole weight. The crack stayed shut and the turns didn't creep, but the root joint ticked twice, and after I let go I could rock the spar in its lashing about a hair's width.
entries.title: Eighth turn holds

entries.query: frapping turns tighten lashing between two poles
entries.text: Read that after the wrapping turns of a lashing you wind frapping turns between the two poles, around the wraps, to cinch them tight. My root joint has wraps and no fraps; that's the rock.
entries.title: Wraps need fraps

entries.text: Snapping stalks at the stand, the smoke past the water came thicker and smelled like something cooking that wasn't acorns. Gathered an armful anyway; frapping takes more cord than I have.
entries.title: Something cooking

entries.text: Twisted the armful into two-ply on the crate: four arm-lengths. Two of the stalks were punky inside and crumbled in the twist.
entries.title: Four arm-lengths

entries.reason: He reads a fix and tries it the same hour.
entries.text: Wound six frapping turns between the two poles around the root wraps, one boot on the stand to pull each tight. The wraps drew in a finger's width and the spar quit rocking under my thumb.
entries.title: Six fraps

entries.text: First hang: no tick, no rock. Second hang, the top frapping turn sawed on the sharp edge of the filed notch and one ply of it parted.
entries.title: Quiet, then a ply

entries.onMind: rounding the notch and cutting canvas strips
entries.query: protect lashing cord from chafing on sharp edge parceling
entries.reason: A joint that holds for one hang and frays on the second isn't a joint.
entries.text: Read that sailors protect rope by parceling it, winding strips of cloth around it before the cord goes on, and that a hard edge should be rounded off. I have a file and an oily square of canvas.
entries.title: Parcel it

entries.query: parceling rope canvas strips overlap direction with the lay serving against the lay
entries.source: National Park Service: Worm, Parcel, Serve
entries.text: Read the old rule: worm and parcel with the lay, then turn and serve the other way. Each strip goes on overlapping the last like shingles, wound the same way the cord twists, so the cord on top doesn't roll it loose.
entries.title: With the lay

entries.reason: His stomach was louder than the tablet.
entries.text: Ate a third of what's left of the loaf and four apple rings on the crate. In the cloth now: a quarter loaf, the cheese wedge, one strip of jerky, five apple rings.
entries.title: Counting the bundle

entries.text: The smoke past the water thinned out while I ate and then just stopped, no fat puff of a fresh feed after it. Whoever keeps that fire let it die on its own this time.
entries.title: Let it go

entries.text: Unwound the top frap, the one with the parted ply, and took the rasp to the lip of the notch. Twelve strokes and a thumbnail slides over it without catching.
entries.title: Twelve strokes

entries.reason: The only cloth he has is doing two jobs, and the wing joint is the one that can break.
entries.text: Tore two finger-wide strips off the edge of the canvas over the compass lid. The shade is a hand narrower now; the needle will have to put up with it.
entries.title: Robbing the shade

entries.text: Parceled the spar at the root joint the way the cord twists, each turn of strip over half the last, and laid a fresh frap over the cloth. It sits snug; the hang waits until I've seen it hold overnight.
entries.title: Shingled

entries.query: how to cut the bottom off a glass jar with string
entries.reason: The lid's cover needs a window, and the honey jar is the only glass he can spare.
entries.source: Instructables: Cut Glass Bottles Using a String
entries.text: Read that you can cut a bottle by tying a string soaked in something that burns around it, lighting it and turning the bottle, then plunging it into cold water so the glass cracks along the hot line. The cut edge comes out sharp and has to be sanded.
entries.title: Fire and cold water

entries.text: I have lamp oil and a whole creek of cold water. What I don't have is an empty jar; it's still half full of honey.
entries.title: Honey first

entries.text: Ate honey off a finger until the jar was down by a third. The rest goes on the bread at supper so none of it gets burned off.
entries.title: Rationing the other way

entries.text: Twisted one arm-length of thin two-ply, finer than the frapping cord. It has to soak up oil and burn evenly all the way around, or the crack will wander off the line.
entries.title: Thin cord

entries.text: Soaked a hand of the thin cord in lamp oil, wound it once around a spar stick and lit it. It smoked more than it burned and went out at the knot, two-thirds of the way around. Cost me a thimble of oil.
entries.title: Smoldered out

entries.query: string bottle cutting flame goes out uneven crack how many wraps
entries.reason: His test cord went out partway around.
entries.source: Instructables: Cut Bottle With Fire and String
entries.text: Read that people wind the string three to five times around, use something that burns hot and fast, and keep the bottle turning so the heat goes all the way around. Lamp oil is slow fuel; more turns and more turning are the parts I can do.
entries.title: More turns

entries.text: Snapped another armful at the stand on the east bank, short dry breaks low on the stems. Five turns around a jar this size is close to two arm-lengths of thin cord.
entries.title: Another armful

entries.text: Twisting the new fibers thinner than this morning's cord, since a thin cord soaks through faster. Half an arm-length so far, and one ply keeps slipping.
entries.title: Finer still

entries.text: Two arm-lengths of thin cord done. Fixed the slipping ply by laying new fibers in alongside its end for a thumb's length; it holds when I pull.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.text: The frap and canvas have sat since last night. Hung off the root joint twice: no tick, no rock.
entries.title: Root joint quiet

entries.text: Third hang I bounced. The joint said nothing, but the stand's left leg kicked out sideways, the frame dropped a hand with a long creak, and I came down on my boots. The wing's fine. The stand isn't.
entries.title: The stand gave

entries.query: bottle cutting with string kerosene instead of acetone does it work
entries.reason: His lamp-oil test cord smoldered out.
entries.source: Instructables: How to cut a bottle with string and nail polish remover
entries.text: Read that people soak the string in thin, quick fuels like nail polish remover so the flame runs all the way around at once. Lamp oil needs a wick to burn, so the cord has to be the wick: thin, loose, and wet all the way through.
entries.title: Fast fuel

entries.text: Spread the rest of the honey on two slices of bread and scraped the jar clean with a finger. Bread's down to a heel and a bit of cheese.
entries.title: Honey on bread

entries.query: how to stop a wobbly wooden stand leg kicking out diagonal brace stake
entries.reason: The stand's left leg kicked out on a bounce.
entries.source: Engineer Fix: How to Stop a Swing Set From Swaying
entries.text: Read that swing sets stop swaying with diagonal braces that make triangles, and with anchors driven into the ground at each leg so the feet can't walk. My stand has neither; the left leg just sits on dirt.
entries.title: Triangles and anchors

entries.text: Pulled a forearm-long stick out of the pile, straight, with one end already broken to a rough point. Good enough for a stake.
entries.title: A stake from the pile

entries.text: White smoke went up past the water, thick at the bottom like a fire just lit. Second fire over there today; whoever it is cooks at odd hours.
entries.title: Smoke again

entries.text: Drove the stake in with the wrench a hand from the left leg. It hit a root halfway down, so I pulled it, moved it a thumb over, and got it in a hand deep.
entries.title: Hit a root

entries.text: Lashed the leg to the stake with one of my two arm-lengths of thin cord, because it was the only cord I had twisted. That leaves one arm-length for the jar, and five turns takes two.
entries.title: Cord spent twice

entries.text: Hung off the frame three times and bounced once. The leg stayed put; the lashing creaks against the stake but holds. One side of the stand is pinned now, the other isn't.
entries.title: It creaks and holds

entries.text: Snapping stalks on the bank, I looked across the water at the brown stalks by the brambles. There's a fresh gap in them, stems broken off low, the ends still pale. Somebody over there is stripping stalks the way I do.
entries.title: Gap on the far side

entries.query: diagonal lashing how to tie cross brace two poles
entries.text: Read that where two poles cross at a slant, you start with a timber hitch around both, wrap one way across the cross, then the other way, then frap between them. A brace has two ends, so that's two lashings, and I have one arm-length of thin cord.
entries.title: Diagonal lashing

entries.text: Twisted an arm-length and a half of thin cord from the armful, which makes two and a half. That's enough for the jar cut or for one end of the brace, not both. The brace goes first; the stand is what I hang on.
entries.title: Jar or brace

entries.text: Yanked a long straight stick out from low in the scrap pile and a sheet of tin slid off the top and clattered down over the rest. The stick is good and straight, wrist-thin, but about an arm shorter than I'd like for a brace.
entries.title: Pulled it loose

entries.query: how much rope is needed for a diagonal lashing
entries.text: Read the rule of thumb for lashings: about three feet of rope for every inch of both poles together. The leg and this stick come to an inch and a half or so, which is roughly two of my arm-lengths per lashing.
entries.title: Three feet an inch

entries.text: Two and a half arm-lengths of cord, two per end. That's one end of the brace and half an arm-length left over. Nothing for the jar.
entries.title: One end, then

entries.text: Ate the last strip of jerky and the five apple rings on the crate. In the cloth now: a heel of bread and a bit of cheese. After that it's the acorn tin.
entries.title: Counting the bundle

entries.text: Because the stick is short, its foot sits close to the leg and the brace stands steep. Lashed the top to the right leg: timber hitch, wraps both ways, three fraps; two arm-lengths gone. The bottom just rests on the dirt, which makes it a stick leaning on a leg, not a brace yet.
entries.title: Short and steep

entries.text: Pointed a stub off the scrap pile and drove it a hand deep with the wrench, right where the brace foot lands. The foot sits against it, but round on round: one lean on the frame and the foot rolled off sideways.
entries.title: Round on round

entries.query: brace foot notch against stake without lashing birdsmouth cut
entries.text: Read about the bird's mouth: a V cut into the end of a rafter so it sits down over the beam it rests on instead of sliding off. A brace that only pushes doesn't need cord at its foot if it has a notch to sit in.
entries.title: Bird's mouth

entries.text: Sun's behind the trunks. Trimmed the bench lantern's wick and lit it; the can's still better than half, and it's still one lantern at a time.
entries.title: Bench lantern lit

entries.text: Filed a V a thumb deep into the brace foot and sat it over the stake. It stays when I lean on the frame, but I filed one side steeper, so the brace twists a hair under load. Not hanging on it till the lantern's brighter than this.
entries.title: V a thumb deep

entries.text: Filed the steep face of the V down by lantern light, a stroke at a time, checking against the stake, until both sides took the same bite. Leaned on the frame: no twist.
entries.title: Both faces even

entries.text: Hung off the frame twice: no creak at the foot, no twist, brace stays seated. On the third hang I bounced, the whole frame creaked long, and the stake under the brace leaned a finger toward the leg in the soft dirt. The joint holds; the ground doesn't.
entries.title: Stake gives

entries.text: Hanging there I was facing west, and the fire past the water jumped up bright orange through the trunks, then settled to a steady glow. Someone fed it right as it got dark.
entries.title: Fed at dark

entries.text: Ate the heel of bread and the last of the cheese on the crate and folded the cloth. Tomorrow it's the acorn tin and whatever I can find.
entries.title: Bundle's empty

entries.text: Knocked the stake down with a fist-sized stone, about twenty blows. It went half a hand deeper and then rang dull and stopped: root or rock under it. That's as deep as it goes in this spot.
entries.title: Hit a root

entries.text: Hung off the frame and bounced three times. The stake didn't lean, the brace stayed seated in its V. The splinted side spar creaked on the third bounce, but the turns didn't move.
entries.title: Holds on a bounce

entries.text: Twisted the last of the stripped fiber into two-ply on the crate: one arm-length, tight, no kinks. The jar cut wants two, so I'm a bundle of stalks short.
entries.title: One arm-length

entries.onMind: a net bag in the creek
entries.reason: The bundle is empty and he's hungry.
entries.text: Ate a handful of the cracked halves out of the tin. Bitter enough to pucker, and they dry my mouth, but they stay down. A tin of still water isn't a creek.
entries.title: Still bitter

entries.text: Carried the bench lantern down to the gray stalks and snapped an armful low, next to last time's gap. Dark tonight, no moon through the clouds.
entries.title: Stalks by lantern

entries.text: Crushed and peeled the stalks on the crate and twisted half an arm-length of two-ply before my fingers went stiff. Some of these stalks were too green and the fiber tears short.
entries.title: Half an arm

entries.text: Set the lantern down by the wing stand, as far from the bench as it goes, and lifted the canvas slow. Four swings, settled, then crept a hair off the line anyway. So it isn't the lantern's heat, or not only that.
entries.title: Not the lantern

entries.text: Looked at the lid side-on with the lantern low: the water isn't domed anymore, it sits a hair under the rim. A whole evening of air did that.
entries.title: Dome's gone

entries.text: Poured water in slow till it humped over the rim. The float slid back to the middle in three swings and stayed. The creep was never the lantern; the water dries down and the float runs to the edge. The lid needs a cover.
entries.title: Brimming again

entries.text: Twisted another quarter arm-length of two-ply from the good fiber and threw the torn green bits on the scrap pile. That's one and three-quarters; the jar cut wants two.
entries.title: Quarter more

entries.text: Set the lantern down on the flat stones in the shallows, the bail clinked, and drank out of my hands. The fire past the water was still going, low and orange through the trunks.
entries.title: Shallows by lantern

entries.text: Twisted the last quarter arm of two-ply and laid it out along the plank twice to check. Two arm-lengths, even, no kinks.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.reason: The jar has to be empty before he can cut it, and he's hungry.
entries.text: Ate honey off two fingers on the crate till the jar was down to the bottom third. While I ate, the fire past the water sank to nothing.
entries.title: Honey and dark

entries.text: Wrapped the new cord around the jar's shoulder: six turns with a hand left over. The page said three to five, so there's cord for a second try if the first burn fizzles, but not while there's honey in it.
entries.title: Six turns

entries.text: Ran a finger round the bottom curve of the jar till there was only a shine left. That was the last of the honey; I'm sorrier about it than I thought I'd be.
entries.title: Last of it

entries.text: Set the lantern on the flat stones and scrubbed the jar with a pinch of creek sand. Held it up to the flame: clear all the way round, one small bubble in the glass near the bottom. Filled it with water to carry back.
entries.title: Clear glass

entries.text: No orange through the trunks past the water, not since before the honey. Whoever keeps that fire is down for the night, earlier than me.
entries.title: Dark past the water

entries.text: The dome had sunk under the rim again and the float was nosing the edge. Poured from the jar till the water humped up; three swings and it sat on center. Until it has a cover, I'm its rain.
entries.title: Topped up again

entries.onMind: burning the jar at first light
entries.reason: He wants to see the cut line and have cold water close when the string burns.
entries.text: Soaked the two-ply in a thimble of lamp oil and wound three turns tight around the shoulder, a finger under the neck, tied flat. Not burning it by lantern; I want daylight on the line and the creek right there.
entries.title: Wrapped for morning

entries.text: Three swings and the sliver sat on center, square to my north notch. No breeze tonight, so the dome holds; what I'm fighting is the water drying down, not wind.
entries.title: Center holds

entries.text: The low owl did its five over the tarp, long-short-short-long-long. The high one answered from past the water, later than most nights.
entries.title: The pair again

entries.reason: He was hungry and it's the only food left in camp.
entries.text: Ate six halves out of the tin. Still bitter at the back of the tongue, and the water in it has gone the color of weak tea; it gets changed in the morning.
entries.title: Six halves
